rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Tables 4 and 8: the authors train and test their own LSTM/GRU/BLSTM/BGRU, CNN, MLP and RF models on a dataset built from 10 years of Fadagosa weather-station data and AquaCrop-simulated tomato and potato yields under fixed sprinkler irrigation depths.
rows.notes: The study reports no result on water saving by a precision/app irrigation scheduling system. Its own result is yield-prediction accuracy (BLSTM MSE 0.017-0.039, R2 0.97-0.99, Table 8) on AquaCrop-simulated seasons; the only irrigation example (Table 10) uses random irrigation amounts and reports net return, not a water-use comparison with traditional methods, and no 30% figure appears. The authors state the model could later be part of a reinforcement-learning irrigation decision system (future work). All yields are AquaCrop simulations never compared with field measurements, so even the prediction result is model-on-model.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Tables 4 and 8: own model runs (BLSTM and comparators) trained and tested on weather-station data plus AquaCrop-simulated tomato and potato yields.
rows.notes: No scheduling system is implemented or evaluated for its effect on yield. The study only shows that a BLSTM can predict end-of-season tomato/potato yield (simulated by AquaCrop) from climate, soil water content and irrigation inputs; it does not show that a scheduling system maintains or improves yield. The yield-prediction model is presented as a component of a future decision-support system, i.e., a precondition of the claimed effect. Yield data are simulated and not validated against field observations.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Table 8: own model runs; potato yield prediction with BLSTM (MSE 0.039, R2 0.988) on AquaCrop-simulated seasons.
rows.notes: The study reports no increase in potato yield (no 15% or any other gain) from a machine-learning-based irrigation system, and does not use real-time soil moisture sensing or report crop quality (size, weight, grade) or water stress. It reports only that a BLSTM predicts AquaCrop-simulated potato yield accurately under different fixed irrigation depths (sandy loam, one site in Portugal). Authors note the models are designed for sandy loam and trained on simulated data (Section 3), but these are limitations of a prediction result, not of the claimed yield-increase effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3, Tables 4 and 8: own model runs on weather data and AquaCrop-simulated yields.
rows.notes: The study contains nothing on disease, waterlogging or soil aeration. It is a yield-prediction modelling paper; the extractor attributed this uncited sentence to [101] by paragraph continuity, but the study provides no evidence on disease risk reduction from irrigation scheduling.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a deep-learning yield-prediction exercise: climate inputs are real station data but yields, soil water content and ETo are AquaCrop simulations under hypothetical sprinkler regimes, never compared with field measurements. It does not implement or evaluate a precision/app irrigation scheduling system, so none of the four claims (water saving, yield maintenance, 15% potato yield gain, disease reduction) is supported by its own results.
